paragraphs.heading: A line a curve keeps approaching
paragraphs.text: An asymptote of a curve is a straight line that the curve creeps toward: the distance between them shrinks to zero as x or y heads off to infinity. The word comes from Greek and means "not falling together". Apollonius of Perga coined it while studying conic sections, though for him it meant any line that never meets the curve.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds
paragraphs.text: Asymptotes come in three kinds: horizontal, vertical and oblique. A horizontal asymptote is a line parallel to the x-axis that the graph approaches as x runs off toward +∞ or −∞. A vertical asymptote is a line at right angles to the x-axis, and near it the function grows without bound. An oblique asymptote is a slanted line, with a slope that is neither zero nor infinite, which the graph approaches as x runs off toward +∞ or −∞.

paragraphs.heading: The curve y = 1/x
paragraphs.text: Take the function f(x) = 1/x, whose points have the form (x, 1/x) for any x other than 0. It passes through (1, 1), (2, 0.5) and (10, 0.1). As x grows to 100, 1,000 and beyond, y shrinks toward nothing, yet 1/x is never 0, so the curve never reaches the x-axis. As x shrinks toward 0, y climbs to 100, 1,000 and more, so the curve rises ever higher beside the y-axis without touching it. Both axes are therefore asymptotes of this curve.

paragraphs.heading: Seen by reason, not by eye
paragraphs.text: A curve getting as close as you like to a line without ever becoming it can feel wrong. On paper or on a screen, though, a drawn line or curve has some width, so if you extended both far enough they would appear to merge. The mathematical line and curve are ideal objects with zero width. Understanding an asymptote takes reasoning, not just looking.

paragraphs.heading: Can a graph cross one
paragraphs.text: Sometimes yes. One function shoots up to +∞ as x nears 0 from the right, which gives it the line x = 0 as a vertical asymptote, and yet its value at 0 is 5. Its graph meets that line once, at (0, 5). A graph can never meet a vertical asymptote more than once, and if the function is continuous everywhere it is defined, it cannot meet one at all. Rational functions supply the usual example of a vertical asymptote: a point where the denominator is zero but the numerator is not.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Asymptotes tell you how a curve behaves far out, and finding them is an important step in sketching a function's graph. The asymptotes met in calculus, mostly of curves of the form y = ƒ(x), can be worked out with limits, and these ideas belong to the foundation of the limit concept. The arctangent, for example, has y = –π/2 as a horizontal asymptote as x tends to –∞ and y = π/2 as x tends to +∞. The Gaussian and logistic functions also have horizontal asymptotes.
